questions.sub_topic: Partnership Deed — Interest on Partner's Loan
questions.question: If the partnership deed is silent regarding the rate of interest on a partner's loan to the firm, the rate of interest payable as per the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 is:
questions.explanation: Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, in the absence of any agreement on interest on partner's loan, interest is payable at 6% per annum.

questions.question: Under the Fixed Capital method of maintaining partner's capital accounts, the capital of each partner:
options: B) Fluctuates with profit, salary, and drawings
C) Remains constant unless capital introduced or withdrawn
D) Always increases with profit share
questions.explanation: In the Fixed Capital method, the capital remains unchanged unless additional capital is introduced or capital is withdrawn. All other adjustments go through the Current Account.

questions.question: P and Q are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3:2. Their capitals are Rs. 90,000 and Rs. 60,000 respectively. The net profit for the year is Rs. 45,000. What is Q's share of profit?
questions.explanation: Q's share = Rs. 45,000 x 2/5 = Rs. 18,000. Profit is divided in the profit-sharing ratio 3:2, not in the capital ratio.

questions.question: A and B are partners. A's annual salary is Rs. 8,000. B gets commission of 10% of net profit after salary but before charging commission. The net profit before salary is Rs. 1,00,000. What is B's commission?
questions.explanation: Profit after salary = Rs. 1,00,000 - Rs. 8,000 = Rs. 92,000. B's commission = 10% x Rs. 92,000 = Rs. 9,200.

questions.question: X and Y are partners with capitals of Rs. 1,10,000 and Rs. 70,000 respectively. Interest on capital is allowed at 8% per annum. What is the total interest on capital charged to P&L Appropriation Account?
questions.explanation: Interest on X = Rs. 1,10,000 x 8% = Rs. 8,800; Interest on Y = Rs. 70,000 x 8% = Rs. 5,600; Total = Rs. 14,400.

questions.question: A partner draws Rs. 5,000 at the beginning of each quarter. If the rate of interest on drawings is 10% per annum, the interest on drawings for the year is:
questions.explanation: Total drawings = Rs. 5,000 x 4 = Rs. 20,000. For quarterly drawings at beginning, average period = (12+9+6+3)/4 = 7.5 months. Interest = Rs. 20,000 x 10% x 7.5/12 = Rs. 1,250.

questions.question: A and B are partners sharing profits in 2:1. Capitals: A Rs. 4,00,000, B Rs. 2,00,000. Interest on capital @ 5% p.a. Salary to A Rs. 20,000 p.a. Commission to B 10% of profit after all adjustments. Net profit before adjustments Rs. 3,00,000. What is B's commission?
questions.explanation: Interest on capital: A = Rs. 20,000, B = Rs. 10,000 (total Rs. 30,000). Net profit before commission = Rs. 3,00,000 - Rs. 30,000 - Rs. 20,000 = Rs. 2,50,000. B's commission = 10% x Rs. 2,50,000 = Rs. 25,000.

questions.question: Which of the following items is NOT shown in the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account?
questions.explanation: Interest on partner's loan is a charge against profit and is debited to the Profit & Loss Account, not the P&L Appropriation Account.

questions.question: Goodwill of a business is classified as a/an:
questions.explanation: Goodwill is an intangible asset representing the reputation, brand value, and benefit of a business.

questions.question: A, B and C share profits in the ratio 3:2:1. They admit D for 1/5th share acquired from old partners in their old profit-sharing ratio. The sacrificing ratio is:
questions.explanation: When the new partner acquires his share from old partners in their old profit-sharing ratio, the sacrificing ratio equals the old ratio. So sacrificing ratio = 3:2:1.

questions.question: Super profit is calculated as:
options: A) Total profit / Number of years
D) Capital employed x Normal rate of return
questions.explanation: Super Profit = Average Profit - Normal Profit. Normal Profit = Capital Employed x Normal Rate of Return.

questions.sub_topic: Goodwill Valuation — Capitalization of Super Profit
questions.question: Capital employed is Rs. 8,00,000, normal rate of return is 10%, and average profit is Rs. 1,20,000. Goodwill under the capitalization of super profit method is:
questions.explanation: Normal profit = Rs. 8,00,000 x 10% = Rs. 80,000. Super profit = Rs. 1,20,000 - Rs. 80,000 = Rs. 40,000. Goodwill = Super Profit / Normal Rate = Rs. 40,000 / 10% = Rs. 4,00,000.

questions.question: On retirement of a partner, the amount due to him (if not paid immediately) is transferred to:
options: C) Capital A/c of remaining partners
questions.explanation: When a partner retires and the amount due is not paid immediately, it is transferred to the Retiring Partner's Loan Account.

questions.question: On admission of a partner, unrecording discovered liabilities are:
questions.explanation: Unrecorded liabilities reduce the net worth of the firm, so they are debited to the Revaluation Account.

questions.question: The excess of assets over liabilities of a business is called:
questions.explanation: Capital = Assets - Liabilities. This is the fundamental accounting equation.

questions.question: A, B and C share profits in 4:3:2. C retires. A and B decide to share future profits equally. The gain of A and B respectively is:
When a new partner brings his share of goodwill in cash on admission, the correct journal entry is:
options: A) Cash A/c Dr.; To Partner's Capital A/c
B) Cash A/c Dr.; To Goodwill A/c
C) Cash A/c Dr.; To Premium for Goodwill A/c
D) Goodwill A/c Dr.; To Cash A/c
questions.explanation: When goodwill is brought in cash by the new partner, Cash A/c is debited and Premium for Goodwill A/c is credited.

questions.question: On dissolution of a partnership firm, the first account that is prepared is:
questions.explanation: On dissolution, the Realisation Account is prepared first to record the transfer of assets and external liabilities.

questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, accumulated profits and reserves are transferred to:
questions.explanation: Accumulated profits and reserves belong to partners and are distributed to their Capital Accounts in the profit-sharing ratio.

questions.question: On dissolution, the balance (profit or loss) of the Realisation Account is transferred to:
questions.explanation: Profit or loss on realization is transferred to the Partners' Capital Accounts in their profit-sharing ratio.

questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, which of the following items is NOT transferred to the Realisation Account?
questions.explanation: Partners' Capital accounts are not transferred to Realisation A/c. They are settled separately after all realizations.

questions.question: On dissolution, assets (book value Rs. 2,50,000) were realized for Rs. 2,00,000. Liabilities (book value Rs. 50,000) were settled at Rs. 40,000. Realization expenses were Rs. 5,000. The profit or loss on realization is:
questions.explanation: Loss on assets = Rs. 2,50,000 - Rs. 2,00,000 = Rs. 50,000. Gain on liabilities = Rs. 50,000 - Rs. 40,000 = Rs. 10,000. Realization expenses = Rs. 5,000. Net loss = Rs. 50,000 + Rs. 5,000 - Rs. 10,000 = Rs. 45,000.

questions.question: On dissolution, if a partner's capital account shows a debit balance, he is:
options: A) Liable to pay to the firm
D) A creditor of the firm
questions.explanation: Debit balance in partner's capital means he owes money to the firm and is liable to pay the deficiency.

questions.sub_topic: Insolvent Partner — Garner vs Murray Rule
questions.question: A, B, C share profits 2:2:1. On dissolution: Assets (book value Rs. 5,00,000) realized for Rs. 4,00,000. Liabilities (book value Rs. 2,00,000) paid in full. Realization expenses Rs. 15,000. C's capital was Rs. 80,000. C is insolvent and cannot pay anything. What is the final amount received by A (capital Rs. 2,50,000)?
questions.explanation: Loss on realization = Rs. 1,00,000 + Rs. 15,000 = Rs. 1,15,000. Distributed in 2:2:1: A = Rs. 46,000, B = Rs. 46,000, C = Rs. 23,000. C's capital after loss = Rs. 57,000 (deficit). Borne by A & B equally: A bears Rs. 28,500. A's final = Rs. 2,50,000 - Rs. 46,000 - Rs. 28,500 = Rs. 1,75,500.

questions.question: On dissolution, debit balance of Profit & Loss Account represents:
questions.explanation: Debit balance of P&L Account represents accumulated losses of the business.

questions.question: As per SEBI guidelines, the minimum subscription required for the issue of shares is:
questions.explanation: As per SEBI guidelines, minimum subscription should be 90% of the issue. If not received, the company must refund the application money.

questions.question: Which of the following CANNOT be done using the Securities Premium Account?
options: B) Issuing fully paid bonus shares
C) Writing off discount on issue of shares/debentures
questions.explanation: Securities Premium can be used for issuing bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, writing off discount on issue of shares/debentures. It CANNOT be used for paying dividends.

questions.question: A company forfeited 100 shares of Rs. 10 each (Rs. 8 called up) for non-payment of final call of Rs. 3 per share. The maximum discount allowed on reissue of these shares is:
questions.explanation: Amount called up = Rs. 8, final call unpaid = Rs. 3, so amount already received = Rs. 5 per share. Maximum discount on reissue cannot exceed the amount already paid on forfeited shares = Rs. 5.

questions.question: Debentures issued by a company represent:
questions.explanation: Debentures are debt instruments representing borrowings of the company. Debenture holders are creditors, not owners.

questions.question: A company issued 1,000 debentures of Rs. 100 each at a discount of 10%. The total amount of discount on issue of debentures is:
questions.explanation: Discount per debenture = 10% x Rs. 100 = Rs. 10. Total discount = 1,000 x Rs. 10 = Rs. 10,000.

questions.question: The correct journal entry for issue of shares at a premium is:
options: A) Securities Premium A/c Dr.; To Share Capital A/c
B) Bank A/c Dr.; To Share Capital A/c
C) Share Capital A/c Dr.; To Bank A/c
D) Bank A/c Dr.; To Share Capital A/c & Securities Premium A/c
questions.explanation: When shares are issued at premium, Bank is debited with the total amount received, Share Capital is credited with the face value, and Securities Premium is credited with the premium amount.

questions.question: A company issued 5,000 shares of Rs. 10 each at a premium of Rs. 2 per share. Application money was Rs. 3 per share, allotment money Rs. 4 (including premium), and first & final call Rs. 5. A shareholder holding 200 shares failed to pay allotment and call. His shares were forfeited. Later, 150 shares were reissued as Rs. 8 paid up at Rs. 6 per share. The amount transferred to Capital Reserve is:
questions.explanation: Amount received on forfeited shares = Application money = Rs. 3 x 200 = Rs. 600. For 150 shares reissued: forfeited amount = Rs. 600 x 150/200 = Rs. 450. Discount on reissue = (8-6) x 150 = Rs. 300. Capital Reserve = Rs. 450 - Rs. 300 = Rs. 150.

questions.question: The balance of Forfeited Shares Account is shown in the balance sheet under:
questions.explanation: The balance of Forfeited Shares Account is shown under Reserves and Surplus as Capital Reserve.

questions.sub_topic: Issue of Debentures — Loss on Issue
questions.question: A company issued 2,000 debentures of Rs. 100 each at a discount of 10%, redeemable at a premium of 5%. The amount of loss on issue of debentures is:
questions.explanation: Loss on issue = Discount on issue + Premium on redemption = (10% x Rs. 2,00,000) + (5% x Rs. 2,00,000) = Rs. 20,000 + Rs. 10,000 = Rs. 30,000.

questions.question: A company has current assets of Rs.12,00,000 and current liabilities of Rs.4,00,000. What is the current ratio?
A company has Current Assets of Rs. 6,00,000, Current Liabilities of Rs. 3,00,000, and Inventory of Rs. 2,00,000. The quick (liquid) ratio is:
questions.explanation: Quick Assets = Current Assets - Inventory = Rs. 6,00,000 - Rs. 2,00,000 = Rs. 4,00,000. Quick Ratio = Rs. 4,00,000 / Rs. 3,00,000 = 1.33 : 1.

questions.question: The debt-equity ratio is used to measure the:
questions.explanation: Debt-Equity Ratio = Long-term Debt / Shareholders' Fund. It measures the long-term solvency of the company.

questions.question: A company's Net Sales are Rs. 20,00,000, Cost of Goods Sold is Rs. 14,00,000, and Operating Expenses are Rs. 3,00,000. The operating ratio is:
questions.explanation: Operating Ratio = (COGS + Operating Expenses) / Net Sales x 100 = (Rs. 14,00,000 + Rs. 3,00,000) / Rs. 20,00,000 x 100 = 85%.

questions.question: Operating Profit Ratio is calculated as:
options: A) Net Profit / Net Sales x 100
B) Gross Profit / Cost of Goods Sold x 100
C) Gross Profit / Net Sales x 100
D) Operating Profit / Net Sales x 100
questions.explanation: Operating Profit Ratio = (Operating Profit / Net Sales) x 100. It measures the operational efficiency and profitability of the business by showing the percentage of net sales generated as operating profit.

questions.question: Common size financial statements show:
options: A) Only absolute figures with trends
B) Each item expressed as a percentage of a common base
C) Percentage changes from the previous year
questions.explanation: Common size statements express each item as a percentage of a common base (total assets for balance sheet, total revenue for income statement).

questions.question: A cash flow statement is divided into how many types of activities?
questions.explanation: As per AS-3, the Cash Flow Statement shows cash flows from three activities: Operating, Investing, and Financing.

questions.question: Purchase of machinery by a company is classified as a/an:
questions.explanation: Purchase of fixed assets like machinery is an Investing Activity because it involves acquisition of long-term assets.

questions.question: Return on Investment (ROI) is calculated as:
options: B) Net profit before interest and tax / Capital employed x 100
C) Net profit after tax / Capital employed x 100
questions.explanation: ROI = Net Profit Before Interest and Tax / Capital Employed x 100. It measures overall profitability relative to capital invested.

questions.question: The most commonly used spreadsheet software for accounting and data analysis is:
questions.explanation: Microsoft Excel is the most widely used spreadsheet application for accounting tasks, data analysis, and financial modeling.

questions.question: In MS Excel, which function calculates the compound interest for a loan?
questions.explanation: FV (Future Value) calculates compound interest over periods

questions.question: In a spreadsheet, depreciation under Straight Line Method or Written Down Value Method can be calculated using:
options: D) Using the SLN() or DB() function
questions.explanation: Excel provides SLN() for Straight Line Depreciation and DB() for Declining Balance depreciation functions.

questions.question: In Excel, the function used to calculate the periodic payment for a loan (EMI) is:
questions.explanation: The PMT() function in Excel calculates the periodic payment for a loan based on constant payments and a constant interest rate.

questions.question: Tally (ERP 9) is a computerised accounting system that provides:
options: B) Automated voucher entry and ledger management
questions.explanation: Tally ERP 9 is a comprehensive accounting software that automates voucher entry, ledger management, financial reporting, and inventory management.

questions.question: In a Computerised Accounting System, payroll module primarily handles:
options: D) Automated calculation of salary, deductions, and payslip generation
questions.explanation: Payroll module in CAS automates salary calculation, statutory deductions (PF, ESI, TAX), and generates payslips.

questions.question: The main advantage of a Computerised Accounting System over manual accounting is:
options: D) Speed, accuracy, and automatic generation of reports
questions.explanation: CAS offers significant advantages in speed, accuracy, automatic report generation, data storage, and easy retrieval.
